# There’s no place like home for All-American wrestler Aaron Smith

By JORDAN HALE  
Staff Reporter

Highline wrestler Aaron Smith is a returning All-American who is looking to conclude his final season as the best wrestler.

Smith’s final goal is to win a national title.

Wrestling began for Smith in middle school his eighth grade year.

“Growing up I always watched my older brothers wrestle, and that is where it all started from for me,” said Smith.

Smith wrestled all four years in high school for Kent-Meridian. He placed in the state 4A tournament two of his four years, including a third-place finish his Senior year.

To be dubbed an All-American wrestler you must go to the national tournament and place in the top 8, and that is exactly what Smith accomplished last year as a freshman at Highline.

Robert was an 18 year old labourer when he enlisted in the Australian Army on 6 Sep 1915. # Book Summaries: FAITH ON THE MARCH – A H MacMillan

By historyofthewtbts / August 5, 2026

# Faith on the March — A. H. Macmillan (1957)

Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, N.J. 259 pages. Introduction by N. H. Knorr, President, Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Pennsylvania.

Two summaries follow: a one-page overview, and a detailed summary of roughly one sentence per page of the original, organised under the book’s own chapter titles.

## One-Page Summary

Faith on the March is the memoir of Alexander Hugh Macmillan (1877–1966), written in his eightieth year after more than half a century inside the organisation that became Jehovah’s Witnesses. Its claim on the reader’s attention is positional rather than literary: Macmillan lived at the Brooklyn headquarters from 1901, was Russell’s designated assistant, went to federal prison with Rutherford in 1918, and was still resident at Bethel under Knorr when he wrote. Knorr’s introduction frames the book as more than one man’s story, noting approvingly that Macmillan “reveals Jehovah’s witnesses as human,” admits their mistakes, and explains why no human organisation can be infallible. That framing is worth holding onto, because the book is a sanctioned account: Macmillan wrote it with permission to use the Society’s files, and Knorr read the manuscript for technical accuracy.

The narrative divides into three movements. The first traces origins — Macmillan’s Nova Scotia boyhood, his sister’s death from diphtheria, an abandoned seminary track and a nervous breakdown, his conversion at a Moody revival, and then his discovery of Russell’s The Plan of the Ages in a Boston meeting hall. Interleaved with this is Russell’s own story: the Allegheny teenager so troubled by eternal torment that he chalked Bible texts on sidewalks, who tested the creeds, abandoned the Bible for his father’s clothing business, and was drawn back by a chance evening in a dusty mission hall around 1870. This section culminates in 1914, and Macmillan’s handling of that year is the book’s most revealing passage. He does not pretend the expectation was met. He quotes his own embarrassing prediction that he was delivering his last public address, describes Russell announcing at breakfast that the Gentile times had ended, and then argues that the error lay in where the Kingdom was established — in heaven rather than on earth — not in the date.
On February 12, 1918, Canada banned several of the Society’s publications including The Finished Mystery, and he quotes the Winnipeg Tribune linking the censor’s order directly to a denunciation from a Presbyterian pulpit. The following day, United States secret service agents seized the Society’s books at Hicks Street in Brooklyn and found nothing detrimental. On February 24, 1918, Rutherford delivered “The World Has Ended—Millions Now Living May Never Die” at Clune’s Auditorium in Los Angeles, fixing much of the blame for the war on religious leaders who had taught the divine right of kings for fifteen hundred years. The Los Angeles Morning Tribune gave the lecture a full page, the ministerial association met the same day to demand an explanation from the paper’s manager, and three days later Army Intelligence occupied the Los Angeles headquarters. Macmillan then documents a legislative campaign, arguing the prosecution was engineered rather than incidental. The Selective Draft Act of June 15, 1917, exempted religious conscientious objectors, and Rutherford’s advice to inquiring young men went no further than telling them to register and file for exemption under Section 3. General James Franklin Bell visited Rutherford to press him to instruct the men at Camp Upton to accept any assignment, and was refused. Macmillan reports Bell’s later admission that a 1917 Philadelphia clergy conference had sent a committee to Washington seeking to have Espionage Act cases tried by military courts with the death penalty, and Bell’s parting line that the bill failed because Wilson prevented it, “but we know how to get you, and we are going to do it.” He then traces the France Amendment, which would have protected anyone uttering “what is true, with good motives and for justifiable ends,” through Senate adoption and subsequent removal at the Justice Department’s urging. He quotes John Lord O’Brian’s letter into the Congressional Record stating that the Act’s effectiveness came from treating motive as irrelevant, and naming religious pacifism the most dangerous propaganda in the country. He further quotes an Attorney General memorandum singling out The Finished Mystery by name and alleging the Bible Students’ headquarters were a resort of German agents. The amended Espionage Act passed without the France Amendment on May 16, 1918 — ten days after warrants had already been issued for the arrest of the Society’s officers. Eight men were arrested on May 8, including Rutherford, Van Amburgh, Robison, Martin, Woodworth, Fisher, De Cecca and Macmillan, released on $2,500 bail each.

### 7. Sentenced to Eighty Years for Preaching the Gospel

Before the trial, visitors from a civil liberties organization warned Macmillan that this was not one denomination’s grudge but a coordinated campaign against unpopular minorities. The trial opened June 3, 1918; after affidavits of bias removed Judge Garvin, Harland B. Howe was brought in from Vermont — the same judge O’Brian had commended in the Congressional Record for treating intent as inferable, a fact the defendants did not know. The government’s theory was that The Finished Mystery had been written to obstruct the war and that letters to draft-age members furthered a conspiracy. Against Macmillan personally the only evidence was a countersigned check paying for printing a book he might never have seen, plus testimony that he managed the office in Rutherford’s absence. Howe himself observed that no act had been shown beyond the check and said Macmillan would be discharged if no evidence of conspiring appeared. Macmillan reports being told that a government attorney was lobbied in the hallway by former opponents inside the Society, who urged that he was the worst of the group and should not be released. The jury returned guilty verdicts on all four counts after about four and a half hours, and Howe sentenced them the next day, declaring their propaganda more harmful than a division of German soldiers and their punishment deservedly severe. Seven received eighty years on four concurrent counts, amounting to twenty years in Atlanta, with De Cecca later given forty. Macmillan’s account of prison is unexpectedly warm: bedbugs in Brooklyn’s Raymond Street jail, buttonhole work in the tailor shop, a guard reducing the six-foot-four Rutherford to tears through the kindness of Italian and Jewish prisoners who finished his jacket for him. He tells of unwittingly buying a stolen bread box for a safety razor and being summoned by the Deputy Warden, and of telling him that if their teaching was false they belonged in prison, but if true, God help the government that persecuted them. The Deputy sat with his head bowed and was later overheard repeating “Macmillan is right,” after which the men were treated with consideration and permitted to teach Sunday school classes — Macmillan’s being fifteen Jewish men studying the promises to Abraham. He closes with the January 1919 election, when he told Rutherford that their absence let Jehovah rather than men choose the president, and Rutherford, re-elected by telegram, vowed to crush creature worship even if it got him kicked out.


### 9. Jehovah Chooses and Cleanses His Channel

Macmillan pauses the historical narrative to trace a change in how Witnesses understood the channel through which God dispenses truth. He offers a self-incriminating anecdote: as a young man he asked Russell whether angels visited his study to explain things to him. Russell, amused, put his hand on his Bible and said everything necessary was there, that he was a student of prophecy but not a prophet, and that light would grow brighter as they kept studying. When admirers said they wished they knew as much as he did, Russell told them it was their own fault, since he printed everything he knew. Another memory reinforces the point: after preaching three times in one day at Cleveland in 1901, Russell refused a sleeping berth on the train, saying that if the friends must stay up all night, so would he. He is unusually frank about the scriptural gymnastics involved: they applied to Russell personally the man with the inkhorn in Ezekiel, the smitten shepherd of Zechariah, the “faithful and wise servant” of Matthew 24, and even Revelation 19:10. He puts the choice starkly: support the present system or fit oneself for God’s new world, with no middle course and a widening chasm that will eventually close. The practical steps he lists are investigation, faith, repentance, approach to God through Christ’s ransom, unconditional dedication, and baptism by total immersion, followed by training that comes from studying the Bible rather than years of expensive study of philosophy and sociology. His picture of the world after Armageddon is domestic rather than apocalyptic: a serene calm, neighbours who mean you well, bodies restored to the freshness of youth, and the dead brought back — you will be working in your garden and hear a familiar voice calling from the room you prepared for your parents. He ends by turning his own tests into questions for the reader: if the Bible contradicted what you have always believed, which would you follow; if you had to choose between a dearly loved individual and your Creator, what would you decide; if worship were forbidden and might cost your life, what would you do. He says he has faced each of these decisions and is more determined than ever, that it has made life worth living, and that it is still helping him face the future without fear.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
